work.text: Sargent is usually not thought of as an Impressionist painter, but he sometimes used impressionistic techniques to great effect. His Claude Monet Painting at the Edge of a Wood is rendered in his own version of the Impressionist style.

Broken touches, here and there broken colour, lightness of key, harmony of tone, unity of effect, and contrast reduced to its lowest terms—the [characteristics], in fact, associated with Impressionism are found in the studies of this period.

source.author: Evan Charteris
source.title: John Sargent
source.publisher: Charles Scribner's Sons, New York (Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: Degas, Renoir, Sisley and Pissarro were among those he saw most often, but Claude Monet was the artist of all others with whom he was on the most friendly terms.

source.author: Evan Charteris
source.title: John Sargent
source.publisher: Charles Scribner's Sons, New York (Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: Although the British critics classified Sargent in the Impressionist camp, the French Impressionists thought otherwise. As Monet later stated: "He is not an Impressionist in the sense that we use the word, he is too much under the influence of Carolus-Duran."

matters.text: Cher Monet je vous remercie et je vous aime. Comme artiste, alors, je vous adore.
